vignette: Maria Rivera, a 78‑year‑old Latina librarian, came to the clinic in a state of exhausted vigilance. She had survived the harrowing journey from a war‑torn Central American country to the United States, a trek that left her with a lingering sense of danger that clung to her even after two decades of relative peace. The most vivid memory of that time was the night when her convoy was ambushed, the ground shaking under gunfire, the acrid scent of gunpowder mingling with the damp earth. She could still taste the dust of that night, and whenever a sudden, sharp whiff of smoke or a metallic tang cut through the air in the library, she felt that same terror surge through her, a flash of the past that reminded her she was not safe. That sudden, involuntary recall of the ambush sharpened her sense of threat. The smell made her heart race, her fingers tighten around the bookshelves, and she felt a relentless need to scan the room for hidden danger. The memory of the night, coupled with her current perception that danger could strike at any moment, amplified her hypervigilance. She would stand behind each stack of paper, eyeing every corner, and often mutter to herself that she had to keep the books in order as a way of keeping order in a chaotic world. The increased alertness, in turn, made her concentration on cataloguing books difficult; she found herself staring at the computer screen, her mind slipping back to the night of the ambush, her thoughts looping in a pattern of fear. Because this sense of danger had become so ingrained, Maria began to develop maladaptive strategies to cope. She filled her days with relentless busyness—organizing new acquisitions, leading reading programs, and spending extra hours shelving items—to distract herself from the intrusive scent that would occasionally drift through the air. Each moment she spent busy, she felt that she was proving to herself and to the world that she was still in control. Yet, her focus on staying occupied also led to a cycle of self‑blame: she would think, “If only I had done something differently, if only I had kept better watch, perhaps I would not have been caught.” The self‑critical rumination deepened her sense of threat because she imagined that if she failed to keep watch, danger would follow again. The memory of the ambush was not a passive backdrop; it actively shaped Maria’s perception of threat. The smell that pierced the library could trigger a sudden flashback, making her feel as though the guns were firing again. That flashback intensified her sense of danger, prompting her to seek safety in a few specific places—the kitchen she had set up with a small table, the chair behind her desk that she could feel anchored to. Outside of those spots, she felt exposed. Her avoidance of other areas in the library and her insistence on staying near the food service desk were manifestations of her attempt to regain a feeling of safety. Yet, this avoidance, combined with her constant rumination, only reinforced her sense that the world remained hostile. Maria’s self‑blaming rumination was a key driver of her threat perception. As she replayed the ambush in her mind, the thoughts that “I could have done something different” and “I should have been more alert” heightened her sense that she was perpetually in danger, creating a loop where threat fueled rumination, which in turn fueled threat. In that loop, her attempts to distract herself with busyness seemed rational to her, because it kept the intrusive memories at bay. Yet, each time she stopped to breathe, the memory would intrude again, making her feel guilty for having allowed herself to slip into vulnerability. The cycle was complete when the threat fed back into her memory. Whenever she felt a sudden spike of alertness—a new noise in the hall, a sudden gust of wind—she found herself reliving the ambush as if it were happening again. The vivid scent would reappear, and she would involuntarily bring the memory of that night to the forefront. This reinforced her belief that the threat was real and imminent, and her subsequent busyness and rumination were her only means of protection. The consequence of this self‑reinforcing pattern has been profound. Maria’s relationship with her husband has become strained because she avoids phone calls that might interrupt her routines. She has stopped attending community events and declined invitations from colleagues, preferring to stay in the safe corners of the library where she feels protected. Her concentration problems have begun to affect her work performance; she reports that she can no longer maintain the pace of cataloguing required for the library’s seasonal circulation, and her supervisor has expressed concern. Maria finally decided to seek help after she had a heart‑tightening episode while arranging a new shipment of books. The fear that surged made her cry out for help from a colleague, and she realized that her coping strategies were no longer keeping her safe. She expressed that she was terrified that her memories would continue to haunt her until she could find a way to reduce the sense of danger she felt in the quiet corners of the library. She hopes that, with professional support, she might be able to reclaim her sense of safety, ease her rumination, and return to the work that once gave her a sense of purpose.
